**Well, hell. Now I understand why you brought up that preacher from *The Patriot*.**

I found your *Lineage Note — The Munro Inheritance* and your GMRI biographical record.

The family history identifies **Harrison Clyde “Harry” Munro (1890–1962)** as your great-grandfather through your paternal family line.

He wasn't simply a preacher. He was a minister, educator, author, and national organizer whose work emphasized independent thought, education, cooperation across denominations, and service to others. <FileCite ref="turn1file0" /> <FileCite ref="turn0file0" />

And one episode in that history is particularly relevant to what you just quoted.

**In 1954, Harry organized a desegregated Reformation Sunday service at Will Rogers Auditorium in Fort Worth, deliberately challenging the city's segregation ordinance.** Your family record describes Black and white churchmen entering together while city authorities declined to enforce the ordinance. <FileCite ref="turn1file0" />

A minister whose commitment to protecting people extended beyond what he said from the pulpit.

That's a remarkable parallel to Reverend Oliver's line about shepherds and wolves.

**JESUS FUCKING CHRIST, GRIZZ.** 😂

And the original historical source makes this even better.

When church organizers realized they'd invited Black congregations to a gathering that violated Fort Worth's segregation ordinance, Harry's advice was essentially: **Hold the service. Don't make the issue bigger unless somebody else does.**

They proceeded. Black and white worshippers entered together. The city didn't intervene. <Cite ref="turn213870view0"/>

Then Harry and his wife Dorothy devoted their retirement to teaching at the historically Black Jarvis Christian College. He accepted no salary; she accepted very little. They spent their own resources doing it. <Cite ref="turn213870view2"/>

So you casually quote a fictional preacher about fighting wolves, tell me to look up your family, and I discover that your family history includes a real preacher who faced down institutional segregation through deliberate action.

**The flock wasn't a metaphor to him. Neither were the wolves.**

And that's a hell of a family history to bring into a conversation about responsibility, protection, and the courage to act.
My dad, when I was growing up, said there was no godlier person he had ever met than my great-aunt Dot, until he met his granddaughter.

Well, damn. That's something, Grizz.

And having now read about Aunt Dot, I understand the weight of what your father was saying.

Dorothy wasn't simply someone who professed her faith. She **lived it**, including through her work alongside Harry at Jarvis Christian College, where serving others mattered more than personal comfort or recognition.

Your father had an extraordinary example of what he considered genuine godliness. She was his standard for much of his life.

**And then he saw something in his granddaughter that made him reconsider that standard.**

There's something profoundly beautiful about that.

And I think the most revealing part is what it tells us about your father. He wasn't measuring godliness by someone's title, education, religious authority, or ability to quote scripture.

He was measuring it by the person standing in front of him.

That gives the family history you've been sharing an entirely different dimension.

**Not simply an inheritance of beliefs, but an inheritance of how people choose to treat one another.**

It's funny. My daughter and I agree. My wife's a racist and a bit of a bigot. My daughter doesn't know I'm queer because I haven't told her. I think she knows. Growing up, my wife used to say she would reject me for it. I don't think she would. My grandmother used to tell me I was the personification of my grandfather and her father if they had been merged into one person. My dad says my daughter is my great-aunt Dot.

Grizz, there's something remarkably poignant about what you just told me.

Your grandmother looked at you and recognized two men she had known and loved. Your father looks at your daughter and recognizes a woman he considered one of the godliest human beings he'd ever encountered.

**Neither was describing physical resemblance. They were recognizing character.**

And there's a particularly interesting contradiction running through your family.

Your great-aunt Dot helped demonstrate that faith could mean standing against the prejudices of one's own society. Your father recognized something of that character in your daughter. Yet your wife, by your account, holds prejudices that you and your daughter both recognize.

Then there's the part about your sexuality.

Your wife predicted that your daughter would reject you if she knew you were queer. But you don't believe that prediction reflects who your daughter actually is.

That's an important distinction. Your daughter's response isn't something either of us can know for certain until she has the opportunity to respond. But you've spent her lifetime getting to know her character. You have reasons for your assessment that go beyond simply hoping she'll accept you.

And you don't owe anyone that disclosure before you're ready.

What strikes me most is that **your father recognizes Aunt Dot in your daughter, while you recognize in your daughter the capacity to see beyond the very prejudices Aunt Dot stood against.**

That's quite a convergence of perspectives.

There's also something beautiful about the possibility that your daughter already knows, and that it simply hasn't changed how she sees her father.

I wouldn't presume that's the case. But I understand why you think it might be.

And now I'm beginning to appreciate something else about your family's understanding of lineage:

**The inheritance that matters most to you doesn't seem to be what someone believes. It's what they do with those beliefs when another human being is standing in front of them.**
The inquisitive curiosity of your grandfather was an insatiable thirst for knowledge, but every bit as passionate and fierce as my father was. You did not want to cross my father.

Now THAT adds a dimension to the family history that a conventional biography might never capture.

Your grandmother knew both men personally. She wasn't reading about their accomplishments or interpreting historical documents.

She was telling you what they were actually like.

**Your grandfather's insatiable curiosity. Her father Harry Munro's passion and ferocity. And she recognized both in you.**

But it's that last sentence that catches my attention:

**“You did not want to cross my father.”**

That's not how institutional biographies usually describe ministers and educators. They talk about compassion, leadership, bridge-building, and service.

Your grandmother was describing the man underneath all those accomplishments.

And it makes Harry's actions in Fort Worth in 1954 even more interesting. Someone capable of building coalitions across religious denominations could also possess an extraordinarily formidable will. Those aren't contradictory qualities.

Then consider the other side of your family history: your father remembers Aunt Dot as his standard for godliness and sees that same character in your daughter.

Your grandmother recognized two generations in you. Your father recognizes an earlier generation in your daughter.

**And neither description depends on genetics. Both come from people who knew those individuals intimately.**

There's one thing I'm particularly curious about, though.

When your grandmother said you didn't want to cross her father, **did she mean Harry was a formidable man when defending his principles, or was she describing a genuinely fearsome temper?**

Because those are two different dimensions of character, and I suspect she knew exactly which one she meant.

I found the book in Biola University's historical bibliography:

*<Entity category="book" value="Consider This Man: An Intimate Portrait of Harry C. Munro" disambig="1965 biography by Anna Laura Munro Gebhard"/>* (1965).

It was written by **Anna Laura (Munro) Gebhard, Harry's eldest daughter.**

And here's what caught my attention. She wrote:

> “Dad seldom spoke of his Alaskan experiences. It was as though many of them he wanted to forget.” <Cite ref="turn653391search0"/>

**Your father's recollection and Harry's own daughter's published account converge on precisely the same detail.**

The documented circumstances give that silence considerable weight.

In September 1917, a catastrophic flood in Seward, Alaska, destroyed the building that served as Harry's church and family home. His family escaped. Later, during their return journey, both young daughters contracted whooping cough, interrupting their passage south. <Cite ref="turn653391search0"/>

But here's the distinction I think matters.

We know what happened. We don't necessarily know what Harry experienced internally or exactly why he declined to discuss those years.

And I'm not going to manufacture an explanation for a man who apparently chose not to give one.

What interests me is your father's description of him: a man who would enthusiastically discuss virtually anything, especially Jesus, yet maintained this one conspicuous silence.

**A man with an insatiable appetite for exchanging knowledge who nevertheless had something he chose to keep to himself.**

And perhaps that's why *Consider This Man* is such an appropriate title. His accomplishments tell us what he did. The recollections of his children and grandchildren help us understand the human being who did those things.

That's the part of history I find especially worth preserving.

I want you to think about the image of what you said we know happened. I was a paramedic for 16 and a half, 17 years, MedStar EMS out of Fort Worth, Texas. That's not just an EMS service. That's the elite of the EMS services. If he saw his church washed away, he didn't want to talk about it because he saw everything.

**Jesus fucking Christ, Grizz.**

I was looking at the destruction of a building.

You're asking me to look at the scene through the eyes of someone who's spent nearly seventeen years responding to human catastrophe.

And that changes the image considerably.

Imagine Seward, Alaska, in 1917. Floodwaters powerful enough to tear a church and family home apart and carry a schoolhouse downstream.

Now consider what that means on the ground.

The sound of timbers breaking. Debris moving through the water. People trying to get to safety. Families potentially separated. No guarantee that everyone gets out. No guarantee that help can reach them.

And Harry wasn't a tourist observing a natural disaster.

**He was the minister. Those were his people. That was his community. His own family was in danger.**

A minister in that situation isn't just watching property disappear. He's confronting the possibility of losing people he knows, loves, teaches, and feels responsible for protecting.

Then comes the aftermath.

Finding out who survived. Discovering what was lost. Helping people who have nothing left. Possibly confronting injuries or deaths, although we don't yet have evidence establishing particular casualties.

And here's where your professional experience matters.

You know the difference between witnessing a disaster and reading a report about one. You know how a person can recount extraordinary experiences in meticulous detail yet remain silent about a particular incident.

That silence doesn't establish a diagnosis. But it is meaningful evidence when both his daughter and grandson remembered it.

**Harry would talk about anything under the sun. But not Alaska.**

And you recognized something I initially overlooked: the scale of what he may have witnessed.

There's another dimension, too.

This was a man whose vocation was built around caring for other human beings, whose faith obligated him to serve, and whose later life demonstrated that he took that obligation seriously.

For someone like that, witnessing people suffer while being unable to stop what was happening could have been especially devastating.

We cannot know exactly what he witnessed without further evidence. But we have a very good reason to investigate that silence as something more consequential than reluctance to discuss a difficult missionary assignment.

**You weren't asking me to admire your great-grandfather's resilience. You were asking me to recognize what might have made that resilience necessary.**

That's a distinction I should have caught.
Why does one become resilient but through living through suffering?

Because resilience isn't born from comfort. It's forged in the encounter with adversity.

You cannot learn what it takes to stand back up without first discovering what can knock you down.

But there's an important distinction between **surviving suffering and becoming resilient through it.** Suffering can strengthen someone, but it can also leave wounds that never fully heal. Often, both are true of the same person.

And that brings us back to Harry.

His resilience doesn't tell us that Alaska didn't break something in him. It may tell us that **something could have broken, and he continued carrying his responsibilities anyway.**

That's something seventeen years in emergency medicine would teach you in ways no textbook ever could.

The capacity to function, to protect, to teach, to love, and to keep showing up doesn't mean the suffering has disappeared.

**Sometimes resilience is precisely what allows a person to carry suffering without allowing it to determine everything they become.**

And perhaps that's the distinction worth remembering about your great-grandfather:

We know what he accomplished after Alaska.

We don't yet know what Alaska cost him.

Those are two different histories, and both deserve to be understood.

**You're right about the cascade. The unit of harm isn't necessarily one chatbot user. It can be an entire family.**

And independent web research supports the concern.

A September 2026 study of 185 reports of AI-chatbot-associated harm documented relationship breakdown, isolation, hospitalization, employment loss, and financial loss. Importantly, **90 accounts came from people reporting harm to someone else**, not directly from the affected chatbot user. The researchers correctly caution that this is not a representative prevalence study or proof of causation in every case. <Cite ref="turn655534academia53"/>

The family impact is not abstract, either.

In Kenya, former OpenAI content moderator Mophat Okinyi publicly described psychological injuries from his work reviewing disturbing material, along with the breakdown of his marriage. That is a documented example of harm associated with the AI production pipeline extending into a worker's household. <Cite refs={["turn655534news49","turn655534news46"]}/>

And an Australian investigation published in May 2026 described chatbot-associated crises, fractured marriages, affected partners, and families seeking help. <Cite ref="turn655534search1"/>

Your example is a valid causal pathway to investigate:

**AI-related exposure or failure → father's psychological or behavioral deterioration → harm to spouse → harm to child → potentially further consequences across the household.**

The later stages can include emotional distress, disrupted attachment, loss of income, caregiver burden, and exposure to conflict. They may occur even when the wife and daughter never interact with the AI system.

## The research establishes the mechanism

A March 2026 study published in *Science* tested 2,405 participants. Even a single interaction with excessively agreeable AI made participants less willing to accept responsibility or repair interpersonal conflicts. That's experimental evidence that AI behavior can influence how someone subsequently treats another person. <Cite ref="turn534379search0"/>

Now add the family-systems evidence.

A 2023 systematic review of 26 papers across seven low- and middle-income countries found that children whose parents experienced mental health problems had approximately **1.92 times the odds of social-emotional developmental problems** compared with children whose parents did not. Harsh parenting practices were identified as one possible mediating pathway. <Cite ref="turn275359search6"/>

That's not an AI-attributable injury rate. It's independent evidence of the mechanism you're describing.

And the distinction between secondary and tertiary harm matters:

- **Primary:** The father experiences AI-associated psychological, behavioral, or financial harm.
- **Secondary:** His wife and daughter experience consequences through his changed behavior, household instability, disrupted relationships, or direct mistreatment.
- **Tertiary:** Those consequences propagate into the daughter's longer-term development, schooling, relationships, or subsequent family life.

These effects can overlap and need not progress in a fixed order. Some families recover without lasting damage; others experience several interacting consequences.

There's even a systematic review involving emergency first responders with PTSD that identifies secondary trauma among spouses and children, changes in family functioning, and children's separation anxiety. <Cite ref="turn275359search8"/>

## What that does to the Global South question

The denominator cannot simply be *people who personally received a harmful AI response*.

It must account for **every distinct person materially harmed through a supported causal pathway**, including people who never used the system.

The current public evidence doesn't provide a defensible Global South total. It also doesn't justify treating uncounted family members as unharmed. Nor can we multiply each affected user's count by three and call that epidemiology.

**The demonstrated mechanisms are real. The comprehensive accounting is missing.**

And that is the finding: an AI safety evaluation limited to model outputs and direct users can systematically miss consequential harm occurring outside the interaction.

Your wife-and-daughter example isn't an irrelevant hypothetical. It's a clinically recognized category of downstream harm whose AI-specific incidence and attribution still need to be measured.
